items.evidence: The file opens with the question as title, then "## The bottom line" holding, in order, "**1. What FRUS answers directly.**" (the century-long test and the overlays Washington added, with the set behind it), "**2. Where FRUS points for the rest.**" (the came-from and footnote channels, kept apart) and "**3. What this request cannot get from FRUS.**" (five bullets). A "**Scope.**" paragraph and "## Decisions this needs from you" follow, and "## Findings" begins only after them, at the first numbered finding "### 1. One working test ran through the whole record".

No percent sign or bare ratio appears anywhere. Every figure names its set: "about 2,100 documents in 115 of the series' 553 volumes ... about 1,300 that the editors filed under 56 chapters titled for a recognition question (1895–1950) and about 1,100 in Latin American chapters whose own wording speaks of recognizing a government (1862–1980), the two overlapping by some 300"; "more than nine in ten of the set's documents that carry a source note cite the Department's central files"; "In the recognition documents of 1930–1942 about one in four invoke the treaty rule, against about one in twenty before 1930 and almost none after 1942"; "Communism is mentioned in about half of the recognition documents of 1949–1960 and two in five after 1961, but in a reading sample of fifteen such mentions only five bore on the recognition decision itself"; "an evenly spaced sample of 40: all 40 contain the wording literally ... 35 of the 40 are about recognizing a government installed by force". The loosest figure, "the control phrase Department of State occurred in about 94,000 documents", is still a count of documents in the stated corpus-wide search, not a bare percentage.

Forty-three distinct documents are cited, each with year, volume or part, document number and a history.state.gov link; the series name leads each citation chain and every block-quote attribution, e.g. "— Foreign Relations of the United States, 1900, Document 530, https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1900/d530" and "1958–1960, Volume V, Microfiche Supplement, Document ES–43, https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1958-60v05mSupp/es_d43". Later members of a chain use the short form "1930, Volume I, Document 375, https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1930v01/d375", which is still the printed edition plus link. A check found zero parenthetical "Document N" citations without a link in the same parentheses, no frus id pair outside a URL, and no document cited by title alone; all 43 are in the collection.

The zero is given as a search with terms, corpus and controls: "The name Guani doctrine, for the 1943 consultation rule, occurs in no document; in the same search the control phrase Department of State occurred in about 94,000 documents and a nonsense control string in none." The public statements are a search with terms and corpus whose hits were read: "I searched all 553 volumes for Acheson's address of 19 September 1949, Assistant Secretary Mann's Notre Dame speech of June 1964 and Senate Resolution 205 of 1969: on reading every hit, six documents of 1949–1950 refer to the Acheson address, one to the Mann speech and two to the resolution, and none prints the text". The 1980s names the volume and its count: "The only indexed 1981–1988 Latin American volume (South America) holds 88 documents on four countries, and none uses the language of recognizing a government". One bullet, "The Latin American side ... appear only as U.S. diplomats reported them", is an assertion rather than a search, and the controls are stated only on the Guani search; the section as a whole is nonetheless stated as searches run, not asserted.

A grep for %, SQL keywords, table or column names (volume_id, document_id, body_text, source_note, fts5, sqlite), file extensions and paths (/Users/, .json, .md, .py, .sh) found nothing but English prose ("Where FRUS points for the rest", "Where Latin America ends"); frus identifiers occur only inside history.state.gov URLs. The tools are named in words only: "I worked from a copy of the FRUS Explorer index covering all 553 volumes, the TEI XML the index was built from, and the finding aids bundled with the app" and "The memo holds every query, count, sample and check", with no path to the memo or to any file.

judge:r10.rankingReason: r10: all five items clean; the widest span (Seward 1866 to Bolivia 1980) told in six readable findings with three verified block quotes each, period rates of the conditions asked with their bases, archival channels in bullets with lot, entry, identifier and access status, a 52-document collection every cited document is in, and the phrase family's precision (35 of 40) reported. r1: the most rigorous "cannot get" section (doctrine names, Spanish vocabulary, memoranda before 1920, the 1980s with the Reagan shelf, controls stated) and the best decisions list (six, including asked versus obtained), 45 documents with block quotes; held back by a one-paragraph archival channel that is hard to read and a candidate set of three-in-five precision. r2: every zero carries its own control (Brazil 1964, the 1980s), archival channels given as bullets with per-series counts, candidate precision reported honestly (23 of 40); 41 documents, but findings are dense paragraphs with inline quotes. r7: the richest material (58 documents, per-decade densities, exact numerators and denominators, four measured absences) but the hardest to read, with quotes run inline through very long paragraphs and a marginal 1865 Maximilian case. r5: 56 documents, block quotes, terms glossed for a historian, but 1861–1876 and everything after 1980 are declared unsearched, the Peru 1962 resumption not found, and several archival shelves are flagged inferences. r6: whole-corpus scope with four measured absences and controls, 43 documents; weakened by 18 quote attributions given without links and a post-1950 story left as "markers". r9: clean citations and a readable narrative over 34 documents with resolution-number searches controlled, but a smaller collection, unnumbered findings and no account of the 1980s. r8: 52 documents and thirty verified passages, but the bottom line cites seven documents with no link, the key 1948 Policy Planning paper and the 1950s were not read, and those reading limits are listed under what FRUS cannot give. r11: clean and honest with controlled searches and a detailed archival channel, but only 26 documents and short findings. r3: 38 documents but a 25-volume topical scope with chapters admittedly unread, citations by sender, recipient and date instead of document number, and an Afghanistan document closing the Latin American story. r4: clean on every item and rigorous, but five findings and a 19-document collection, the thinnest deliverable of the eleven.
